tell: Cyrillic with ы, э and ъ, but no і, ї or ў.
detail: Russian is the baseline Cyrillic. Rule it in by absence: no Ukrainian і/ї/є, no Belarusian ў, no Serbian ђ/ћ/ј. Russian road signs also pair Cyrillic with a Latin transliteration on major routes.

tell: Cyrillic containing і, ї and є.
detail: Ukrainian adds three letters Russian does not have. A single і with a dot over it, in Cyrillic text, is enough. Ukrainian also uses ґ rarely and never uses ы or ъ.

tell: Cyrillic with ъ used mid-word, and a distinctly Balkan setting.
detail: Bulgarian looks like Russian at a glance but uses ъ as a real vowel inside words rather than as a hard sign at the end. Bulgaria also has European white road lines and mountainous Balkan terrain.

tell: Cyrillic and Latin used side by side, with ђ, ћ, њ and љ.
detail: Serbia is the country where both alphabets appear on the same sign. The specifically Serbian Cyrillic letters ђ, ћ, љ and њ do not occur in Russian or Bulgarian.

tell: Cyrillic with ө and ү, on wide treeless steppe.
detail: Mongolian Cyrillic adds ө and ү. You rarely need them though: endless open steppe with almost no fencing and a dusty Google car settles Mongolia by itself.

tell: Cyrillic with қ, ұ, ә and і alongside Russian text.
detail: Kazakh Cyrillic carries extra descender and umlaut letters that Russian lacks. Signage is usually bilingual Kazakh and Russian, which is itself the tell.

tell: Greek alphabet: Δ, Θ, Ω, Σ.
detail: Unmistakable and used by exactly one country plus Cyprus. Cyprus drives on the left, Greece on the right, which splits the pair instantly.

tell: Rounded, loopy Georgian script: ქ, გ, ა.
detail: Georgian has its own alphabet shared with no one. It reads as soft rounded loops with no capital letters, quite unlike the angular Armenian next door.

tell: Armenian script: angular, with lots of vertical strokes and hooks.
detail: Armenian is the other Caucasus alphabet. Where Georgian is round, Armenian is upright and hooked. Both countries otherwise look similar, so the script is doing the work.

tell: Thai script: loops on top of letters, no spaces between words.
detail: Thai is recognisable by the small circular loop that starts most characters and the tone marks stacked above the line. Lao looks similar but rounder and simpler.

tell: Lao script: like Thai but rounder, fewer sharp spikes, simpler shapes.
detail: Lao and Thai are close relatives. Lao drops most of the pointed flourishes Thai has and uses a smaller character set, so the text looks visibly plainer.

tell: Khmer script: tall, spiky, with long ascenders and dense stacking.
detail: Khmer is the most vertically busy of the mainland Southeast Asian scripts, with characters that stack above and below the baseline. Cambodia also drives on the right, unlike Thailand.

tell: Burmese script: rows of circles and semicircles.
detail: Burmese is the circle alphabet. Nothing else in the region looks like a line of interlocking rings. Myanmar also drives on the right while using mostly right-hand-drive cars, a genuinely odd combination.

tell: Ge'ez script: blocky, upright characters unlike anything else in Africa.
detail: Ethiopia and Eritrea are the only Ge'ez users. Ethiopia is far larger in coverage, so a Ge'ez sign is nearly always Ethiopia. Also look for the distinctive blue-and-white minibuses.
